prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its translation into long-acting incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: GLP-1 is the only candidate on which all six of us placed first, and I do not treat that as merit in itself; the merit is that the arc runs unbroken from hormone physiology (Holst on secretion and action of the active peptides, Drucker on the intestinotropic and metabolic biology) to long-acting agonists (Knudsen's acylated analogues, liraglutide and semaglutide) that change outcomes in type 2 diabetes and obesity and show cardiovascular and renal benefit in large independent trials. The mechanism is stable, the impact is global and recognition is timely. A prize that honours both the physiology and the step that made it a medicine reflects what the discovery actually was.
statement.case_against: Credit is the weak point. Four credited names are squeezed into three, Mojsov's contribution on the active peptide is genuinely disputed and I moved away from her only because the priority record is the least settled part of the story, and Habener sits outside the supplied names. Honouring Knudsen with two academic discoverers raises the question of whether an industrial drug-development contribution belongs in a physiology-or-medicine citation, and the class still has open long-term safety questions. If the committee decides the attribution cannot be made defensibly, B006 is the cleaner alternative.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius proposes Drucker, Holst and Mojsov as a basic-science trio, regarding Knudsen's work as major but arguably drug development, while acknowledging priority disputes over early GLP-1 work.
responses.response: I made the same choice in my opening ballot, so I take this argument seriously. On reflection I have changed it. The citation I would defend names a discovery that became a medicine, and that is not clearly a basic-science trio. Knudsen's analogues are what the clinical evidence rests on. Mojsov's claim on the active peptide is real but is the part of the record most contested between laboratories, and I cannot resolve it from the file. I would accept Mojsov in place of Knudsen if the committee prefers a purely discovery-based citation, but I would want that reasoning stated explicitly.

responses.point: Perlmann treats GLP-1 as one of the clearest bench-to-bedside arcs, but says the allocation is not clean, since Mojsov and Habener are contested or outside the supplied credit, and he asks whether we reward the hormone or the drug.
responses.response: I agree on the arc and on the open question. My answer is that the hormone and the drug should both be named in the citation, since neither alone explains the change in clinical practice. I disagree with treating Habener's absence as a reason to hold the candidate back. The three-person limit forces exclusions in almost every case on our list, and a contested edge is not the same as a contested core. Holst and Drucker are secure under any reading.

responses.point: El-Manira ranks optogenetics second, as a causal method that reshaped circuit analysis, and proposes Deisseroth, Hegemann and Nagel, while accepting that it is mainly a research tool with clinical use still emerging.
responses.response: I share the view that the scientific originality is exceptional, and I ranked it third myself. My reservation is attribution. Six people have strong claims, and your trio leaves out Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenböck. Bamberg's early work on the light-gated channel is part of the discovery chain. A prize that excludes him while including the neuronal application is hard to defend as a discovery citation. Until the committee can state a split that holds up, I would put it behind GLP-1 and CAR-T, although I would keep it as a serious alternative.

responses.point: Linnarsson ranks CAR-T second and splice-switching antisense therapy for SMA third. He regards the SMA attribution as clean for Krainer and Bennett, and notes that the CAR-T list omits foundational concept contributors.
responses.response: I agree that the SMA credit is the cleanest on the shortlist, and I ranked it fourth for that reason. I place it below CAR-T because the impact is narrower, and because Bennett's chemistry and Krainer's mechanism are largely a single therapeutic story, not an independent discovery. On CAR-T, I share your concern about Eshhar, and I think it is the main reason a CAR-T prize would be harder to defend than it first looks. If the committee leaves out the original receptor concept, the citation has to be worded around costimulated, clinically validated CARs.

responses.point: Sandberg ranks BCL11A and fetal hemoglobin regulation third, as a clean arc from human genetics to an approved gene-editing therapy, but acknowledges that timing may be slightly early and that the editing tool has its own prize.
responses.response: The genetics-to-cure arc is compelling, and I did not rank B009 on my own ballot, so I would want it on the table for round two if you wish to argue for it. I am cautious on maturity. Casgevy is recent, durability and off-target data are still accruing, and the discovery credit is difficult to separate from the CRISPR contribution that has already been recognised. It may be a candidate for a later year. For now I would not place it ahead of three candidates with more than a decade of follow-up. B009 is also not on the shortlist, so it cannot enter my configuration.

uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers a discovery-only credit (including Mojsov) or a discovery-plus-drug credit including Knudsen, and how Habener should be handled.
Whether the industrial drug-development contribution can be honoured alongside academic discoverers in a physiology-or-medicine citation.
How to split the six credited names for optogenetics, and whether Bamberg's exclusion can be defended.
Whether Eshhar's absence from the CAR-T credit is a decisive weakness for that candidate.
Long-term safety data for the incretin class remain incomplete, and I cannot verify the latest outcome trials independently.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with any shortlisted candidate is apparent from my profile. I trained with Paul Greengard, who is not a candidate, and my profile records about twenty co-authored works with Thomas Perlmann, a fellow committee member, on topics unrelated to the shortlist. I do not regard these as requiring recusal, and I disclose them for completeness. My work in neurology and neuropharmacology is not in an area where I have a personal stake in any candidate.
